name: Paipai
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. ... Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations verified verbatim: Langdon 1977:239 in the now-complete SCOPIL 4 PDF text (previously only a carved JPEG of one page, no copy held) and Sánchez Fernández 2016:30/127-128 in the thesis text we hold. The classification (root stress surfacing as word-final; fixed final, no secondary) is supported by four independent lines that agree: Langdon 1977 (family-level, authoritative), SF2016 (Paipai fieldwork), StressTyp2 via Joël 1966, Gordon 2002 'Final (of root)'; Ibáñez 2017's transcriptions are all final-stressed. Nothing found contradicts it. It is 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced' because the deciding sentence is a pan-Yuman generalization and the two Paipai-specific phonologies (Joël 1966, Ibáñez Bravo 2015) are unheld and not openly available; the record's grade/cite/loc fields are empty. Action: fill cite/loc with the SCOPIL 4 file we hold (p.239, plus p.240 'stress

sources.quote: Sánchez Fernández 2016:30 (Spanish): "Stress will always be on the root, usually on the last syllable in the case of bisyllabic constructions, which makes it possible to distinguish the base in lexemes." (p. 127-128 adds: "stress in Paipai, as in all Yuman languages, falls on the root (Langdon 1975)".)

sources.citation: Ibáñez Bravo, María Elena. 2017. Descripción del estatus fonológico de los segmentos [i̯] y [u̯] de la lengua paʔipá:y. Cuadernos de Lingüística de El Colegio de México 4(1): 181-209.
sources.quote: No stress-placement rule stated; 'sílaba acentuada' used as a given throughout; every cited form is transcribed with final stress (e.g. /ɲukwé/ 'qué', /ɲanmís/, /ɲelpáʃ/ 'miel', p.203). Cites her 2015 ENAH thesis and Mixco n.d. ms as the phonological descriptions.
